p.x:
Dario Amodei talking to the NYT about uncertainty:

'We've been a relatively responsible company. And I think because we focus on enterprise, I think we have a better business model. I think we have better margins. I think we're being responsible about it. 

But again, let's say you have a different business model. Let's say you have a consumer business model. You know, you're kind of, the source of your revenue isn't as good, your margins aren't as certain, and let's say you're a person who just kind of like constitutionally just wants to yolo things, or just likes big numbers. Then you may turn that dial pretty far. 

And so I think there is a real underlying risk. Whenever there's uncertainty, there's a risk of overextension. We all face it. I face it. All the other companies face it. There's an inherent risk when the timing of the economic value is uncertain. There's an inherent risk of underreacting or overextension. 

And because the companies are competing with each other, and frankly we genuinely need to compete with, you know, our authoritarian adversaries. There's kind of a lot of pressure to push things. So I think there's some amount of irreducible risk here, and I absolutely don't want to deny this, but at the same time I think there are some players who are not managing that risk well, who are taking unwise risks'

p.x:
Dario Amodei's 35 mints interview is such a great watch.

He believes simply scaling current architectures, with small tweaks, will yield systems like a country of geniuses in a data center.

Because such capability has national security stakes, he opposes exporting top chips to authoritarian regimes and urges democracies to exploit AI without adopting mass surveillance.

He backs targeted regulation for the largest models, warns of serious job disruption especially for entry roles, and argues companies plus governments must retrain workers and share productivity gains so shorter workweeks and broader prosperity become possible.

Talks about the "cone of uncertainty", i.e. how hard it is to guess future demand and revenue while being forced to make huge spending decisions today.

Anthropic’s revenue has been growing extremely fast, but next year’s number could reasonably be 20 billion, 30 billion, 50 billion or more. That spread is the cone: a wide range of plausible outcomes, not a single forecast.

At the same time, building data centers and buying chips takes 1 to 2 years. So he has to decide now how much compute to lock in for models that will run several years from now, before he actually knows how big the business will be.

If he buys too little compute, Anthropic will have to turn customers away and lose them to competitors. If he buys too much and demand comes in low, the company might not earn enough to pay for all that infrastructure, which in the extreme could threaten its survival.

p.x:
Dario Amodei talks about how the AI labs are dealing with a “cone of uncertainty”.

They are making data center and compute bets now that don’t come online for 2+ years. If they undershoot, competition takes share. If they overshoot, could go bankrupt.

He says Anthropic’s enterprise focus reduces the uncertainty because the margins are much larger than in consumer market.

Even if revenue slows (annual sales have gone from $100m  to ~$10B in two years), Anthropic can better forecast its compute needs in enterprise market and margin cushions the blow from any overspend.
